halden-bank-for-freelancers.title: Halden: a bank account that budgets for you
halden-bank-for-freelancers.excerpt: A banking app for freelancers that sets money aside for tax and rent the moment an invoice is paid.
content: Freelancers are paid on different days in different amounts, and most budgeting apps assume a salary. Halden asked us to design an account that copes with that.
Client: Halden, a bank for freelancers
Services: product design, iOS and Android, web dashboard

Halden had a banking licence and a waiting list of 8,000 freelancers, but no product. They needed an app that felt calm on a bad month and helped on a good one, ready for a launch date their investors had already announced.
Interviewed 24 freelancers about how they handle irregular income
Designed pots that fill themselves by a share of every payment
Built the iOS, Android and web apps on one shared design system
Ran a beta with 400 people for four weeks before launch
41% more weekly active users than their previous budgeting app
Average tax pot covers 96% of the bill by January
4.8 stars from 3,100 ratings in the app stores
Tilework felt like part of our team from the first week. The app shipped on the date they promised.
Ines Novak, Head of product, Halden

mossgrove-outdoor-store.title: Mossgrove: an outdoor store built for phones
mossgrove-outdoor-store.excerpt: Three out of four visits came from phones, but most sales came from laptops. We rebuilt the store around the thumb.
content: Mossgrove makes jackets, packs and boots for people who walk a long way. Their old store looked good on a laptop and fell apart on a phone.
Client: Mossgrove, outdoor clothing and kit
Visitors on phones were adding to the bag and leaving at checkout. Mossgrove wanted a store that sold as well on a phone on a train as on a desk at home, without moving off WordPress.
Watched twelve customers shop on their own phones
Redesigned product pages around photos, sizes and stock left
Cut checkout from five steps to two, with wallets first
Made every page load in under two seconds on a slow connection
38% more of mobile visits end in an order
Returns for the wrong size down by a third, thanks to a fit guide
They asked better questions about our customers than we did. The new store paid for itself in the first season.

quillo-notes-for-teams.title: Quillo: notes a whole team can write in
quillo-notes-for-teams.excerpt: A notes app for teams that had more sign-ups than users. We redesigned the first ten minutes.
content: Quillo had a loyal core of users and a leaky trial: most teams signed up, wrote one note and never came back.
Client: Quillo, notes and docs for teams
The product was good once a whole team was in it. The problem was getting there. Quillo asked us to find out why trials stalled and to fix the first ten minutes.
Studied 60 recorded trial sessions and interviewed 15 teams that left
Replaced the empty first page with templates for real meetings
Made inviting a teammate part of writing the first note
Wrote every empty state and message again, in plain words
2.4 times more trials turn into paid teams
Teams invite their second person within 6 minutes, not 3 days
Support questions in the first week halved
We had been guessing for a year. Two weeks of research told us exactly what to fix.

brisa-coffee-brand.title: Brisa: a coffee brand from the coast
brisa-coffee-brand.excerpt: A name, a sun and a bag you can spot across a shop. The first roast sold out in nine days.
content: Two baristas were opening a roastery by the sea and wanted a brand that felt like a slow morning, not another black-and-gold coffee bag.
Services: naming, brand identity, packaging, website
Team: two brand designers, one engineer
They had a building, a roaster and great coffee, but no name, no packaging and a launch in two months. The brand had to work on a bag, a cup, a van and a small online shop.
Named the roastery Brisa, Portuguese for a sea breeze
Drew a wordmark and a rising sun that works at any size
Chose four colours from the coast: clay, sunrise, espresso and foam
Designed the bags, cups and a small online shop for subscriptions
The first roast of 600 bags sold out in nine days
320 coffee subscriptions in the first three months
Stocked in 14 cafés and shops within the year
People pick the bag up before they know what is in it. That is exactly what we hoped for.

tidal-energy-website.title: Tidal: solar power, explained in one page
tidal-energy-website.excerpt: Solar panels are complicated. Tidal’s new website makes the decision simple, and quote requests tripled.
content: Tidal installs solar panels and home batteries. Their website explained the technology well, and lost people before they asked for a price.
Client: Tidal, home solar and batteries
People wanted three answers: will it work on my roof, what will I save and how long does it take. The old site answered them on six different pages. Tidal asked for a site that answered them in one.
Rewrote the site around the three questions people ask
Built a roof check that gives a saving in under a minute
Refreshed the brand with a sun-yellow and a calmer navy
Set up search pages for the 40 towns Tidal works in
Three times more quote requests each month
Organic visits up 212% in a year
Average time to a quote down from four days to one
Clear prices, no surprises and a demo every other Friday. I have never enjoyed a website project before.

parcel-and-pine-cabin-booking.title: Parcel & Pine: cabins booked in three taps
parcel-and-pine-cabin-booking.excerpt: A family business with 40 cabins and a booking form by email. Now people book on the map, in three taps.
content: Parcel & Pine rents forty cabins in the hills, many of them dog-friendly. Bookings came by email and phone, and every reply took a day.
The family wanted guests to see what was free and book it on the spot, without paying a big booking site a fifth of every stay.
Designed a map that shows each cabin’s price for the dates you pick
Built booking and payment in three steps, with dogs as an option
Connected the calendar to the cleaners’ rota
Trained the family to run it all from WordPress
Direct bookings up 64% in the first season
€38,000 less in booking site fees in a year
Replies to booking emails down from 30 a day to 4
We got our evenings back. Guests book while we sleep, and the cleaners always know where to go.

design-systems-small-teams-use.title: Design systems that small teams actually use
design-systems-small-teams-use.excerpt: A design system is not a big library. For a small team it is twelve parts, written down, that everyone reaches for first.
content: Most design systems we inherit are big and abandoned: three hundred components, half of them used once. Small teams do better with less.
Start with the twelve parts you use every day
Buttons, links, inputs, cards, headings, a grid, colours, spacing, icons, alerts, a modal and a table. Get those right and most screens build themselves.
Write down when, not just how
Every part gets one sentence on when to use it and one on when not to. That sentence prevents more inconsistency than any token.
Name parts after what they do, not how they look.
Keep one source: the code, not a file next to it.
Review new parts once a month, together.
Count how often each part appears in your product. Anything used once is a candidate to delete, not to document.

scope-a-website-in-one-week.title: How we scope a website in one week
scope-a-website-in-one-week.excerpt: Five days, three workshops and one page at the end. Here is how we turn a brief into a fixed price.
content: Clients ask how we can give a fixed price when the work is new. The answer is the first week: we spend it making sure we agree on what we are making.
We meet the team, then talk to five customers. We leave with the visits that matter: who comes, what they came for and what they do next.
We sketch the pages on paper with the team in the room. Arguments are cheap on paper.
Thursday and Friday: write it down
One page: the goal, the pages, what is in and what is out, the plan by week and the price. If it does not fit on one page, the project is too big for one round.

ship-in-two-week-sprints.title: Why we show work every other Friday
ship-in-two-week-sprints.excerpt: Two weeks is long enough to make something real and short enough that nobody drifts. Here is what happens in a demo.
content: Every second Friday, every client gets a demo of real, working things. Not slides. It is the habit that keeps our projects on time.
Thirty minutes. We show what changed, on a link the client can open on their own phone afterwards. Then we agree on the next two weeks.
One week is too short to finish anything worth showing. Four weeks is long enough to go the wrong way for a month. Two is the right size for us.
The demo is the deadline. Everything else is a plan.

fast-pages-without-a-rewrite.title: Fast pages without a rewrite: our checklist
fast-pages-without-a-rewrite.excerpt: Most slow sites do not need a new stack. They need smaller images, fewer fonts and one less script.
content: When a client says their site is slow, they often expect us to suggest a rebuild. Usually an afternoon with this list does more.
Resize and compress images, and serve them in modern formats.
Load one font family in two weights, from your own server.
Remove scripts nobody can explain, one at a time.
Lazy-load anything below the first screen.
Cache pages, and check your host does too.
Test on a mid-range phone over a slow connection, not on your desk. The difference is usually four times.
Add a speed budget to every release: if a page gets slower, it does not ship until it is fixed.
